meta.blurb: Cyrano can fight a hundred men and rhyme at the same time, but he believes no woman could love his enormous nose. When the beautiful Roxane falls for a handsome soldier who cannot speak, Cyrano lends him his words, and his own heart.
meta.bible: Cyrano de Bergerac: a Gascon soldier, poet and swordsman with a huge nose; proud, brave, witty, generous; secretly loves his cousin Roxane. Roxane: Cyrano's beautiful, clever cousin, who loves poetry and fine words. Christian de Neuvillette: a handsome young soldier who is a poor speaker and loves Roxane; he joins the Cadets of Gascony. Comte de Guiche: a powerful nobleman who loves Roxane; he later becomes a duke and admires Cyrano. Vicomte de Valvert: a foolish nobleman who insults Cyrano's nose. Montfleury: a fat actor whom Cyrano drives off the stage. Le Bret: Cyrano's loyal friend. Ragueneau: a pastry cook who loves poetry and lets poets pay in verses. Ligniere: a poet and drunkard, Cyrano's friend. Cadets of Gascony: the company of soldiers in which Cyrano and Christian serve. Hôtel de Bourgogne: the Paris theatre in 1640. Porte de Nesle: the gate where Cyrano fights a hundred men. Arras: the besieged town where the Cadets are sent to war. Paris, France, Gascony, Spanish, Spain. Capuchin: the monk who marries Roxane and Christian. Panache: Cyrano's gallant spirit, symbolised by a white plume. Voice and tone: witty, passionate and heroic, bitter-sweet; set in France in 1640 and fifteen years later in 1655; fights are shown with no gore; Christian dies in battle, and Cyrano dies after a log is dropped on his head by an enemy.

beats.scene: A noisy crowd of nobles, soldiers and pages fills a grand Paris theatre
beats.summary: In 1640 a noisy crowd fills the Hôtel de Bourgogne theatre in Paris, waiting for a play.

beats.scene: Christian looks anxiously at an empty box in the crowded theatre
beats.summary: Christian de Neuvillette, a handsome new soldier, loves a lady he has never spoken to and watches for her.

beats.scene: Ligniere whispers to Christian as the Comte de Guiche enters the theatre
beats.summary: A friend tells Christian that the lady is Roxane, cousin of Cyrano, and that the powerful Comte de Guiche wants her too.

beats.scene: A fat actor starts to speak on stage as Cyrano stands in the crowd
beats.summary: When the actor Montfleury begins to speak, Cyrano stands and orders him off the stage and not to return for a month.

beats.scene: The fat actor hurries off the stage while the crowd laughs and cheers
beats.summary: Cyrano's sword and wit drive Montfleury from the stage, and Cyrano pays the manager for the spoiled play.

beats.scene: A nobleman sneers at Cyrano's huge nose and Cyrano answers grandly
beats.summary: The Vicomte de Valvert mocks Cyrano's nose, and Cyrano answers with a speech of far wittier insults.

beats.scene: Cyrano fights the Vicomte with a sword while speaking a poem
beats.summary: Cyrano fights the Vicomte while making up a poem, promising to hit him at the last line, and he does.

beats.scene: Cyrano speaks sadly to his friend Le Bret in the emptying theatre
beats.summary: Alone with Le Bret, Cyrano admits that he loves his cousin Roxane but believes nobody could love a man with his nose.

beats.scene: An old servant woman brings Cyrano a message in the dark theatre
beats.summary: Roxane's old servant brings a message that Roxane wants to meet Cyrano the next day, and Cyrano is overjoyed.

beats.scene: Ligniere runs up to Cyrano with a frightened face in a dark street
beats.summary: Cyrano learns that a hundred men are waiting to attack Ligniere that night, and he decides to protect him alone.

beats.scene: Cyrano stands alone under a gate and fights many men by moonlight
beats.summary: At the Porte de Nesle Cyrano fights a hundred men alone and wins.

beats.scene: Poets eat cakes in Ragueneau's busy bakery while Cyrano waits
beats.summary: The next morning in Ragueneau's bakery, where poets pay for cakes with poems, Cyrano waits nervously for Roxane.

beats.scene: Cyrano writes a letter at a table and hides it inside his coat
beats.summary: Cyrano has written a love letter to Roxane and hopes to find the courage to give it to her.

beats.scene: Roxane enters the bakery and takes Cyrano's hands with a smile
beats.summary: Roxane arrives and greets Cyrano warmly, and Cyrano hopes for a moment that she loves him, but she has a secret.

beats.scene: Roxane speaks happily about Christian while Cyrano turns pale
beats.summary: Roxane says she loves a handsome Cadet in Cyrano's company and asks Cyrano to protect him.

beats.scene: The Comte de Guiche enters the bakery with guards while Cyrano frowns
beats.summary: The Comte de Guiche offers to help Cyrano with his play, but Cyrano proudly refuses to change a word.

beats.scene: Gascon soldiers crowd in and cheer Cyrano while Christian looks anxious
beats.summary: The Cadets cheer Cyrano, and Christian makes a joke about his nose, but Cyrano controls his temper because Christian is Roxane's love.

beats.scene: Cyrano embraces Christian and tells him a secret in a corner
beats.summary: Cyrano tells Christian that Roxane loves him, and Christian is thrilled but admits that he is a poor speaker.

beats.scene: Cyrano and Christian shake hands as Cyrano gives him a letter
beats.summary: Cyrano offers to give Christian the words while Christian gives the looks, and they agree to woo Roxane together.

beats.scene: Roxane reads a letter by lamplight with a happy smile
beats.summary: Cyrano writes letter after letter in Christian's name, and Roxane loves Christian more with every page.

beats.scene: Christian stands below Roxane's balcony speaking awkwardly while she frowns
beats.summary: Left alone below Roxane's balcony, Christian can only say that he loves her, and she goes inside, disappointed.

beats.scene: Cyrano hides in the dark under the balcony and speaks softly to Roxane
beats.summary: Cyrano, hidden in the shadows, speaks the words for Christian, and Roxane is enchanted.

beats.scene: Christian climbs to the balcony and kisses Roxane while Cyrano watches
beats.summary: Roxane asks for a kiss, Cyrano sends Christian up the balcony to receive it, and Cyrano suffers in silence.

beats.scene: A monk arrives at the gate with a letter while Roxane thinks quickly
beats.summary: A Capuchin monk brings a letter from the Comte de Guiche, and Roxane tricks him into marrying her to Christian.

beats.scene: Cyrano tumbles into the street and tells the Comte he fell from the moon
beats.summary: Cyrano delays the Comte with an outrageous story about falling from the moon until the wedding is done.

beats.scene: The angry Comte de Guiche shouts orders at the Cadets in a street
beats.summary: The furious Comte sends the Cadets of Gascony to the war at Arras, and Cyrano promises Roxane that Christian will write every day.

beats.scene: Thin, hungry Cadets sit in a cold camp outside the walls of Arras
beats.summary: At the siege of Arras the Cadets are cold and hungry, but Cyrano keeps up their spirits.

beats.scene: Cyrano crosses a misty field at dawn toward the enemy lines with a letter
beats.summary: Every morning Cyrano slips through the enemy lines to post a letter for Christian, risking his life.

beats.scene: A grand coach drives into the camp and Roxane steps out smiling
beats.summary: Roxane arrives in a coach full of food, having charmed her way through the Spanish lines, to the joy of the soldiers.

beats.scene: Cadets share food around a fire while Roxane thanks each man
beats.summary: The Cadets feast and sing, and the Comte de Guiche warns that a great attack is coming and decides to stay and fight.

beats.scene: Roxane speaks softly to Christian in a quiet corner of the camp
beats.summary: Roxane tells Christian that she loves his soul as shown in his letters, and he realises that she loves Cyrano's words.

beats.scene: Christian speaks seriously to Cyrano as the grey dawn comes over the camp
beats.summary: Christian asks Cyrano to tell Roxane the truth and let her choose between them.

beats.scene: Christian lies on the battlefield as Cyrano kneels beside him
beats.summary: In the battle Christian is struck down, and as he dies Cyrano whispers that Roxane loves him.

beats.scene: Roxane kneels beside Christian and takes a stained letter from his coat
beats.summary: Roxane finds Christian's last letter over his heart, stained with blood and with Cyrano's tears.

beats.scene: Roxane in black walks into a convent gate while Cyrano watches
beats.summary: Roxane retires to a convent to mourn Christian, and Cyrano says nothing of the truth but promises to visit her.

beats.scene: Roxane in black embroiders in an autumn convent garden among falling leaves
beats.summary: Fifteen years later Roxane still mourns Christian in the convent garden in autumn.

beats.scene: Cyrano walks cheerfully into the convent garden to meet Roxane on Saturday
beats.summary: Every Saturday for fifteen years Cyrano has visited Roxane and amused her with the news of Paris.

beats.scene: Le Bret and Ragueneau speak worriedly to Roxane in the garden
beats.summary: Le Bret tells Roxane that Cyrano is poor and alone and has made many dangerous enemies.

beats.scene: The Duke de Guiche in rich clothes speaks thoughtfully to Roxane in the garden
beats.summary: The Comte de Guiche, now a duke, visits Roxane, admits his admiration for Cyrano and warns her that his enemies are dangerous.

beats.scene: A heavy log falls from a high window onto a man walking below
beats.summary: As Cyrano walks to the convent, someone drops a heavy log on his head from a window, and he hides the wound under his hat.

beats.scene: Cyrano walks slowly into the garden, pale, with his hat pulled low
beats.summary: For the first time in fifteen years Cyrano is late, and Roxane notices that he is pale and weak.

beats.scene: Cyrano jokes with Roxane on a bench in the failing light
beats.summary: Cyrano cheerfully tells the news and gossip of the week, though he is growing weaker.

beats.scene: Roxane gives Cyrano a small cloth bag with an old letter
beats.summary: Cyrano asks to read the last letter that Roxane keeps next to her heart, and she gives it to him.

beats.scene: Cyrano reads a letter aloud as the sun sets in the convent garden
beats.summary: Cyrano begins to read the letter aloud, and the light fades.

beats.scene: Roxane listens in the dark as Cyrano speaks without looking at the page
beats.summary: It is too dark to read, but Cyrano goes on speaking the letter by heart, and Roxane realises that he cannot be reading.

beats.scene: Roxane stands and stares at Cyrano with wide eyes in the dusk
beats.summary: Roxane realises that Cyrano wrote the letters and spoke at the balcony, and she cries out that it was he all along.

beats.scene: Roxane holds Cyrano's hand and weeps as the first stars appear
beats.summary: Roxane weeps because she loved one soul all her life, and it was his, and she has lost him twice.

beats.scene: Le Bret and Ragueneau run into the garden as Cyrano draws a sword
beats.summary: Le Bret and Ragueneau find Cyrano and beg him to rest, but he stands, draws his sword and fights his old enemies in the air.

beats.scene: Cyrano leans on a tree and lifts his head proudly
beats.summary: Cyrano says he will take one thing with him that nothing can take away, his panache, and Roxane kisses his forehead.

beats.scene: Roxane kneels beside the fallen Cyrano as autumn leaves cover the garden
beats.summary: Cyrano dies in the garden, and Roxane is left weeping, with his panache remembered as his true gift.

B1B2: In the year 1640, a noisy crowd fills a theatre in Paris called the Hôtel de Bourgogne. Nobles, soldiers, thieves and poets all push and talk, waiting for the play to begin.
Christian de Neuvillette is a handsome young man who has just joined an army company. He is in love with a lady in the theatre, but he has never spoken to her.
A friend tells Christian that the lady is Roxane, a clever and beautiful woman who is also admired by the powerful Comte de Guiche. The Comte wants her to marry a man he chooses.
When the actor Montfleury begins to speak, a loud voice shouts at him to stop. It is Cyrano, who stands up in the hall and orders the fat actor off the stage for a month.
Cyrano lifts his sword with a smile, and the frightened actor runs off the stage. Cyrano pays the manager for the ruined evening, and the delighted crowd laughs and cheers.
The Vicomte de Valvert, a foolish nobleman, says that Cyrano's nose is very large. Cyrano replies with a long speech of far cleverer insults than anything the Vicomte could think of.
Cyrano challenges the Vicomte to a duel, and he promises to make up a poem as they fight. At the last line of the poem, he says, he will touch the Vicomte with his sword.
When the crowd has gone, Cyrano tells his friend Le Bret his secret. He loves his beautiful cousin Roxane, but he is sure that nobody could love a man with such a nose.
An old servant comes to Cyrano with a message from his cousin Roxane. Roxane wishes to meet him the next day, and Cyrano is so amazed and happy that he can hardly speak.
Ligniere runs up to Cyrano with some terrible news that he has just heard. A hundred men are waiting in the dark to attack him because of a song he wrote, and Cyrano promises to protect him alone.
At the Porte de Nesle, Cyrano stands alone against a hundred men. His sword moves so fast that, by the end of the night, the street is empty.
Ragueneau is a cook who loves poetry, and poets eat his cakes and pay him with verses. Cyrano waits in the shop that morning with a nervous heart, hoping that Roxane will come.
Cyrano has written a love letter to Roxane, because he wants to say what he cannot say aloud. He keeps it in his coat, and he wonders whether he will ever have the courage to give it to her.
Roxane arrives and greets her cousin kindly, as she did when they were children. Cyrano hopes for a moment that she has come to say she loves him, but she wants to tell him a secret.
Roxane says that she loves a handsome young man who has just joined Cyrano's company. She is afraid for him, so she asks Cyrano to look after him.
The powerful Comte de Guiche offers to help Cyrano with his play, but only if Cyrano changes it. Cyrano proudly refuses to change a single word for any man alive.
The Cadets of Gascony come to cheer for Cyrano, and the new Cadet Christian is among them. Christian, trying to seem brave, makes a joke about Cyrano's nose, and everyone waits for the fight.
Cyrano suddenly embraces Christian and tells him that Roxane loves him. Christian is delighted, but he sadly admits that he does not know how to talk to a clever woman.
Cyrano offers to write and speak for Christian, so that Roxane will love the words of one and the face of the other. Christian agrees with joy, and the two become partners in one love.
For weeks Cyrano writes beautiful letters for Christian, and Roxane reads them again and again. She tells Cyrano that she loves Christian more with every page.
Alone with Roxane at her balcony, Christian forgets everything Cyrano taught him. He can only say that he loves her, and she is disappointed and goes into the house.
Cyrano tells Christian to call Roxane back, and he hides under the balcony in the dark. He speaks the words of love, and Roxane believes that they are Christian's.
Roxane asks for a kiss, and Cyrano pushes Christian up the balcony to take it. Cyrano stays in the dark below, and he suffers in silence.
A monk arrives with a letter from the Comte de Guiche, who wants to visit Roxane that night. Roxane tricks the monk into thinking that he must marry her to Christian at once.
When the Comte arrives, Cyrano stops him with a ridiculous story about falling from the moon. By the time the Comte understands, the wedding is over.
The angry Comte sends the Cadets of Gascony to the war at once. Christian must leave his bride, and Cyrano promises Roxane that Christian will write to her every day.
At the siege of Arras the Cadets of Gascony are cold and hungry, because the Spanish have cut off their food. Cyrano keeps up their spirits with jokes and songs.
Every morning before dawn, Cyrano slips through the enemy lines to post a letter to Roxane. He writes it in Christian's name, and he risks his life each time.
A fine coach drives into the camp, and Roxane steps out, smiling. Her coachman is Ragueneau, the pastry cook, and the coach is full of good food for the hungry soldiers.
The soldiers eat and sing while Roxane thanks each man for his courage. Then the Comte de Guiche warns that a great attack is coming, and he decides to stay and fight beside the Cadets.
Roxane tells Christian that she came because of his wonderful letters. She says she would love him even if he were ugly, and Christian realises that she is in love with another man's words.
Christian tells Cyrano that Roxane loves him, not Christian, and he begs Cyrano to tell her the truth. He says that she must be free to choose the man she truly loves.
Christian falls in the great battle, and Cyrano runs to him. As Christian dies, Cyrano whispers that Roxane loves him, and Christian dies in peace.
Roxane kneels beside her husband and finds a letter over his heart. It is a farewell written by Cyrano that morning, and the page is stained with blood and tears.
Roxane decides to live in a convent for the rest of her life, mourning her husband. Cyrano says nothing about the letters, and he promises to visit her every week.
Fifteen years pass, and it is autumn in the convent garden. Roxane, still dressed in black, sits quietly, and she wears Christian's last letter next to her heart.
Every Saturday for fifteen years, Cyrano has come to see Roxane, and he has never missed a visit. He brings her the news of Paris, as a loving friend would.
Le Bret tells Roxane that Cyrano is poor and lonely, and that he has made many powerful enemies. Cyrano says what he thinks, even when it is dangerous.
The Comte de Guiche, now a duke, visits Roxane and speaks of how much he admires Cyrano. He warns her that Cyrano's enemies are powerful, and that one of them may do him harm.
On his way to the convent, Cyrano is hit on the head by a heavy log that falls from a window. He is badly hurt, but he hides the wound under his hat.
For the first time in fifteen years Cyrano is late, and he walks slowly into the garden. Roxane notices that he is pale, but he laughs and says that it is nothing.
Cyrano sits beside her and tells the news of the week in his funny way, although he is growing weaker. Roxane laughs, and then she grows serious and worried.
Cyrano asks if he may read Christian's last letter, the one that Roxane always wears over her heart. After a moment she gives it to him, surprised that he has asked at last.
Cyrano begins to read the letter aloud in a low, tender voice. The sun sets, and the garden grows dark around them.
It becomes too dark to read, but Cyrano goes on speaking, and he does not look at the page. Roxane suddenly realises that he knows every word by heart.
Roxane understands everything at last, and she cries out that it was Cyrano all along. He tries to deny it, but he is too weak, and in the end he cannot lie to her.
Roxane tells Cyrano that she has loved only one soul in her life, and that it was his. She weeps because she has been in mourning for fifteen years without knowing that he was sitting beside her.
Le Bret and Ragueneau run into the garden and beg Cyrano to lie down. Instead he stands, draws his sword and fights bravely against enemies that nobody else can see.
Cyrano says that he knows what he is taking with him, and it is his panache, his proud and gallant spirit. Roxane bends down and kisses his forehead, and at last he is happy.
Cyrano closes his eyes and dies in the quiet garden, holding Roxane's hand. She stays beside him, and the leaves fall softly around them.
C1C2: In the year 1640, the great hall of the Hôtel de Bourgogne in Paris filled with a noisy, glittering crowd that had come to see a famous play. Gentlemen in feathered hats jostled with soldiers, pickpockets slipped through the press, and hungry poets argued about verses while pages dashed about among them. Beneath all the din ran a restless excitement, for everyone seemed to feel that something remarkable was about to happen.

Among the crowd stood Christian de Neuvillette, a handsome young man newly joined to the company of the Cadets of Gascony, who kept glancing toward an empty box as though his whole life depended on it. He had fallen deeply in love with a lady who would soon appear there, and he had never spoken a word to her. He was brave enough to face any enemy, yet the thought of addressing a clever woman filled him with something very close to terror.

A drunken poet named Ligniere, who knew every secret of Paris, told Christian that the lady was Roxane, an educated and charming cousin of the swordsman Cyrano. He added that the powerful Comte de Guiche loved her too, and that the Comte meant to marry her to a foolish nobleman of his own choosing so that he might keep her near. Christian listened with dismay, for he had neither rank nor eloquence to set against such a rival.

No sooner had the famous actor Montfleury begun his speech than a thunderous voice rang out from the crowd, commanding him to be silent. It was Cyrano de Bergerac, soldier, poet and duellist, who had taken a strong dislike to the fat, self-satisfied actor and had forbidden him to appear on the stage for a whole month. The audience gasped and stared, for none dared to cross Cyrano, a man whose sword was as quick as his wit.

Cyrano drew his sword with an easy flourish, and the terrified actor scurried from the stage amid roars of laughter from the delighted crowd. Calmly he offered the manager a purse of money to pay for the ruined evening, since he had no wish to cheat anyone, only to silence the actor. Then he leaned against a pillar, grinning, with a nose so enormous that every eye in the hall had already measured it.

A haughty young nobleman, the Vicomte de Valvert, stepped forward and remarked, with a sneer, that Cyrano's nose was rather large. Cyrano replied that this was a poor attempt, and, to the delight of the hall, poured out a dazzling list of insults he might have used instead, some tender, some savage, and all more inventive than the Vicomte's. No one in the theatre had ever heard such wit, and the Vicomte stood open-mouthed, understanding that he had begun a battle he could not win.

Cyrano offered to fight the Vicomte there and then, composing a ballad as they fought, and promised that at the final line of its last verse he would touch him with his sword. The astonished audience formed a ring around the pair, and Cyrano's blade flashed while his voice recited each line, as lightly as if he were strolling in a garden. At the final word the Vicomte staggered back, touched and beaten, and the crowd roared its delight at the swiftest, wittiest duel that anyone had ever seen.

When the theatre had emptied, the proud swordsman sat down beside his friend Le Bret and, for the first time that evening, let his face fall. He confessed that he had loved his cousin Roxane for years, and that he was certain no woman so lovely could ever look kindly upon a man with such a monstrous nose. Le Bret protested, but Cyrano shook his head with a bitter smile and said that a brave heart was no use when the mirror told the other half of the story.

Just then Roxane's old servant appeared with a message from her mistress, who wished to meet her cousin privately on the following morning. Cyrano, who had never dreamed that Roxane even remembered him, felt himself shaken from head to foot by a sudden, dizzy happiness. He agreed at once to the meeting, and all his gloom of a moment before vanished like mist in the sun.

Ligniere stumbled up with terrible news: for a song that he had written against a powerful man, a hundred hired swordsmen lay in wait for him that night near the Porte de Nesle. Cyrano, who was in the mood to do the impossible, laughed with delight and declared that he would escort the poet home himself. He asked his friends to come and watch, for he intended that the night should be remembered.

At the Porte de Nesle, Cyrano stepped alone into the narrow street and faced the hundred swordsmen who had come to harm his friend. His blade flickered like lightning, and those who did not fall back in alarm fell wounded, so that by the end of that wild night the way was free and Ligniere was safe. All Paris would talk of it for weeks, and Cyrano, who loved a great deed more than any prize, went home with his heart still singing.

Ragueneau's pastry shop was a curious place, for the cook adored poetry more than money and gladly let hungry poets pay for their cakes with verses. There Cyrano waited the next morning, nervous as a boy, listening for the sound of a light step at the door. He had slept little, and he had rehearsed a hundred speeches, and every one of them seemed foolish in the bright morning light.

In the pocket of his coat, Cyrano carried a letter that he had written to Roxane, pouring out all the love he had never dared to speak. He had told himself that today, perhaps, he might find the courage to place it in her hand, and that she might read it and understand. Yet each time his fingers touched the paper, he heard the cruel voice of doubt whisper the one word that had ruled his life, which was nose.

Roxane swept in, bright as sunshine, and greeted her cousin as warmly as she had when they were children together, which made his heart leap foolishly. He began to hope that she had come to say something that would change his whole life, and he listened with all his soul. Then she told him her secret, which was that she was in love, but not with him.

The man she loved, she said, was a handsome, noble young soldier who had just joined Cyrano's own company of Cadets, and whom she had seen only from afar. She trembled for his safety among the fierce, quarrelsome Gascons, and she begged her cousin to protect him from every danger and every duel. Cyrano, pale as paper, heard her out and promised, because he could refuse her nothing.

The Comte de Guiche, the great man whom Roxane feared, strolled in and offered to place one of Cyrano's plays before the cardinal himself, on condition that a few lines should be altered. Cyrano refused with ringing scorn, declaring that he would not change a single comma for the favour of any lord alive and that he preferred to walk alone. The Comte went away with a cold smile, having gained nothing but a powerful new enemy.

The Cadets of Gascony crowded in to cheer their hero, and among them stood Christian, who had been warned that no one in the company dared even to glance at Cyrano's nose. Wishing to prove that he was no coward, Christian made a joke about it, and the whole room fell silent, waiting for the explosion. But Cyrano, white with the effort, clenched his hands behind his back and let the insult go by, for the young man was the one Roxane loved.

To everyone's astonishment, Cyrano suddenly embraced the young man and told him in a low voice that he was Roxane's cousin, and that she loved him. Christian was overjoyed at the news, but his happiness soon clouded, for he admitted with a miserable face that he was a dull speaker, with no gift for pretty phrases or love letters. He feared that the first time she heard him talk, she would wonder what she had ever seen in him.

Cyrano proposed a bargain that was part generosity and part despair, in which he would supply the eloquence and Christian would supply the handsome face and manly bearing. Together, he said, they would make a single perfect lover who would win Roxane's heart completely. Christian agreed with joy, never suspecting what the arrangement cost his friend, and Cyrano, who had planned to speak for himself, now locked his own love away like a treasure he would never spend.

Over the following weeks Cyrano wrote letter after letter in Christian's name, pouring into them all the beauty and tenderness that he could not speak in his own. Roxane read them again and again, kept them close to her heart, and told her cousin with shining eyes that she loved Christian more with every page. Cyrano listened, smiled and suffered, and he came to feel that he was both the happiest and the most miserable man in Paris.

One warm evening Christian stood below Roxane's balcony and, left to himself, discovered that all the fine speeches he had rehearsed had vanished from his head. He could only repeat that he loved her, again and again, in simple words, until she grew impatient and asked him to say it more beautifully. When he could not, she turned away with a disappointed little sigh and went into the house.

Cyrano, who had been waiting nearby, pushed Christian aside, stepped into the shadows beneath the balcony and called up to Roxane in the dark. Because the night was black and his voice was soft, she took him for Christian at his best, and she leaned over the railing to listen to the most beautiful words she had ever heard. He told her of his love with such passion and poetry that he forgot, for a few precious minutes, that he spoke for another man.

At last Roxane, overcome, begged for a kiss, and Cyrano, with a trembling heart, whispered to Christian to climb up to the balcony and take it. As the lovers embraced above him, Cyrano stood in the dark and felt the kiss like a sword turned against his own breast, for it belonged to his words and to another man's lips. Yet he did not speak a word of complaint, and a faint, bitter smile moved on his face.

A Capuchin monk appeared at the gate with a letter from the Comte de Guiche, who announced that he wished to come to Roxane's house that night. Roxane, thinking quickly, read the letter aloud, altered its meaning, and persuaded the innocent monk that the Comte wished her to be married to Christian at once. While the holy man led the couple into the house, Cyrano remained outside to deal with the Comte.

When the Comte de Guiche came hurrying down the dark street, Cyrano, wrapped in a cloak, tumbled in front of him and announced with a perfectly straight face that he had just fallen from the moon. He went on spinning the most absurd and wonderful tale of his journey through the skies, while the Comte grew more and more bewildered. By the time the nobleman saw through the game, the marriage was made and could never be undone.

The Comte de Guiche, furious at being tricked, ordered the Cadets of Gascony to march at once to the siege of Arras, so that Christian was torn from his bride before they had spent a single night together. As he left, Roxane made Cyrano promise to watch over her husband and to make him write to her every day. Cyrano promised, thinking privately that the letters would be the easiest part of the bargain.

At Arras the Cadets of Gascony found themselves besieged as much as besiegers, for the Spanish had cut off their supplies and the soldiers were hungry, ragged and cold. Cyrano walked among them as he always did, with a joke for the weary and a song for the sad, and he made even the empty stomachs forget the empty cupboard for an hour at a time. It was said that he found more courage in a single laugh than other men found in a barrel of wine.

Each morning before daybreak, Cyrano slipped through the enemy lines at the risk of his life and carried a letter to Roxane, written in Christian's name but written by his own heart. Christian, noticing how pale and weary his friend looked, began to wonder what was in those letters that was worth such a perilous journey. Cyrano told him that he did it for love of a good cause, and he said no more, though his hand trembled slightly as he buttoned his coat.

To the amazement of the whole camp, a handsome coach rattled up through the mud, and out stepped Roxane, radiant and smiling, with Ragueneau driving at the reins. She had talked her way across the Spanish lines by sheer charm and courage, and the coach was packed with pies, wine and delicacies enough to feed a hundred starving men. The Cadets cheered themselves hoarse, and for the first time in many days there was singing around the campfires.

The soldiers ate, drank and sang as though they had never known hunger, and Roxane moved among them like a lady at a festival, thanking each man for his courage. But the Comte de Guiche, who had come to the camp with his own troops, warned that a great enemy attack was close, and that this might well be the last night for many of them. He decided to stay and fight beside the Cadets, and the hardened Gascons, who disliked him, found that they respected him a little more.

Alone with Christian, Roxane told him that she had risked everything to reach him because of his letters, which had shown her a soul more beautiful than she had imagined. She declared that she would love him even if he were poor and ugly, since it was the spirit that she adored and not the face. Christian, hearing this, grew very pale, for he understood that it was not he whom she loved, but the man whose words he had borrowed.

Christian went to Cyrano and said, quietly and without anger, that Roxane loved the poet and not the soldier, and that she should be told the truth and allowed to choose between them. Cyrano, shaken to his depths, protested for a moment, but he could not deny the justice of the request, and he promised to tell her at once. He would have done it, too, if the cannon had not begun to thunder across the field at that very moment.

In the first attack of the Spanish, Christian was struck down and carried to the edge of the field, where Cyrano knelt beside him in the smoke. The dying man asked, in a faint voice, whether Roxane loved him, and Cyrano, who had resolved on a lie more generous than any truth, whispered that she did. Christian closed his eyes in peace, and Cyrano remained kneeling, knowing that with his friend had died the last chance he would ever have to speak.

Roxane ran across the field and knelt beside her husband's body, weeping, and found over his heart a last letter that he had carried into battle. It was a farewell of great beauty, written by Cyrano that morning in Christian's name, and the page was stained with blood and with the tears that Cyrano had shed as he sealed it. Cyrano stood silent beside her, bound by his own secret vow, and let her go on believing that the words had been the dead man's own.

After the battle, Roxane resolved to devote the rest of her life to mourning Christian, and she retired to a convent in Paris to live in black among the quiet nuns. Cyrano, who had fought like a lion that day and now felt older than his years, said not one word of the truth, and gave up for ever the chance of being known. He promised to visit her, and he kept that promise with a faithfulness that no army could have forced upon him.

Fifteen years later, on an autumn afternoon, Roxane sat embroidering in the convent garden beneath trees that were dropping their golden leaves one by one. She still wore black for her husband, and next to her heart, in a small bag, she kept the farewell letter that had come to her stained with his blood. The nuns loved her gentleness and the sadness of her beauty, and they respected her long, patient grief.

Every Saturday for fifteen years, Cyrano had come to the convent to sit beside Roxane and amuse her with the gossip of the city, and not once had he failed her. The nuns had grown to love his teasing and his stories, and Roxane had come to regard him as her oldest and most faithful friend, the one man who understood her sorrow. He gave her what she asked of him and never asked anything in return, and she did not know what it cost him.

Le Bret came to Roxane with a worried face and told her that Cyrano was growing poorer and lonelier each year, living in a bare room and refusing every offer of help. His sharp tongue had made enemies of the great, the foolish and the dishonest, and Le Bret feared that one of them would find a way to strike. Roxane smiled and said that Cyrano had always been fearless, but she promised to speak to him.

The Comte de Guiche, who had become a duke, visited the convent garden and talked with Roxane in a voice that had lost much of its old arrogance. He confessed that he had long admired the man who had once defied him, and he warned her that Cyrano's enemies were plotting something, and that an accident might be arranged. Roxane thanked him gravely, and the old rivals parted with a respect that neither of them would once have thought possible.

On his way to the convent that Saturday, Cyrano was struck from behind by a heavy log that someone had let fall from a high window, and he sank to the pavement with blood running from his head. He lay there a while, dazed, and understood that his enemies had at last found their chance. Then, with the stubbornness that had carried him through a hundred battles, he got to his feet, pressed his hat down over the wound and went on.

For the first time in fifteen years Cyrano was late, and when he appeared at last under the falling leaves, he walked with slow and careful steps, a hat pulled low over his head. Roxane, who had been teasing him gently for his lateness, stopped suddenly when she saw how pale he was. He laughed and said that it was an old wound from the war that had decided to pay him a visit.

He settled himself on the bench beside her and began to recite the news of the week in the old comic style, with a gleam in his eye and a joke for every item. Roxane laughed, as she always did, but as the afternoon darkened she saw how his voice thinned and how his hand trembled when he pushed back the hair from his forehead. A cold fear crept into her heart, though she could not have said why.

Suddenly Cyrano asked whether he might, at last, be allowed to read the farewell letter that she carried over her heart, and which he had never been permitted to see. Roxane hesitated, because it was the dearest thing she owned, but something in his voice made her say yes. She took the small bag from her dress and put it in his hand, and he unfolded the stained paper with fingers that trembled a little.

Cyrano began to read aloud, softly at first and then with growing passion, the words of the farewell that he had written fifteen years before. The sun was sinking, the air was turning cold, and the shadows lengthened across the garden until the leaves above them were nothing but dark shapes against the sky. Roxane sat still and listened, moved as she always was by the beauty of those few lines.

When the light failed so completely that the page was only a pale blur, Cyrano went on speaking, and his voice never faltered or hesitated over a single word. Roxane stared at him through the gloom and slowly understood that he could not possibly be reading, that he was reciting the letter from memory. At the same moment she recognised the voice itself, for it was the voice that had once spoken to her from the darkness beneath her balcony.

In a single blinding moment Roxane saw the whole truth: the letters, the balcony, the beautiful words that she had given to another man's name. She cried out that it had been Cyrano all along, and her voice shook with wonder, sorrow and a love that she had carried, without knowing, for fifteen years. He tried feebly to deny it, but the old pride had left him, and there was no more strength in him to pretend.

Roxane wept, and she told him that all her life she had loved only one man, though in her blindness she had given that love to a handsome face. Now, she said, she had lost the soul behind the words twice, once on the battlefield and again in this quiet garden, as soon as she found it. Cyrano gently begged her not to grieve, for he said that he had been happy in his way, since he had been permitted to love her and to be near her.

Le Bret and Ragueneau came running into the garden and pleaded with Cyrano to lie down and let a doctor see him, but he refused. He rose to his feet, drew his sword and began to strike at the air, challenging, one by one, the old enemies that had plagued him all his life: Falsehood, Compromise, Prejudice and Cowardice. He declared that he would fight them to the very end, and he swung his blade with a fierce joy that astonished the onlookers.

Leaning against a tree, he told them that there was one thing which neither time nor death could take from him, and that he would carry it with him untouched into the grave. It was his panache, the gallant spirit of a man who had never bowed or lied or sold his pen, and who had loved the best that he knew. Roxane bent down and pressed her lips to his forehead, and he smiled, as one who has received everything he asked of life.

Cyrano's strength failed at last, and he sank down into Roxane's arms and died there in the quiet garden, with the leaves falling softly around them. He had lived without ever bending his head, he had loved without ever asking for return, and he had gone out of the world as proud and brave and witty as he had come into it. Roxane held him close and wept, and his spirit seemed to remain behind in the gathering dusk like a white plume that no wind could blow away.
